blocks.h: A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

There is a particular sound a person makes when they must not laugh and are going to anyway. It is not the laugh. The laugh is the easy part and it is the same in every country. It is the other thing — the sound of a laugh being held, which comes out of the nose at pressure because every other exit has been sealed, and which is high and thin and ugly and utterly humiliating, and which no adult has ever produced on purpose. You will have made it. In a lecture, in a meeting, at a graveside. And you will remember exactly what your body did around it: the cheeks going, because the pressure has to be held somewhere. The head going down and never back. The hand arriving over the mouth, which people believe is to muffle the sound and which is in fact to hide the shape. The chest pulling in short hard strokes at a rate it was not built for. And then the eyes, which give the whole thing away, because a mouth can be covered and eyes answer to nobody. Here is what I have been unable to put down for two years. That is what grief looks like. Precisely that. The same posture, the same muscles, the same sound. A man doubled forward in a black suit with his face in his hands and his shoulders going and his eyes streaming is either the funniest he has ever been in his life or the saddest, and there is no test available to anybody in the room, including him. We have built a great deal of our public life on the assumption that these two things are opposites. They use the same equipment. They always have. And in a place where a man of a certain kind is never permitted to weep in a room with the lights on, it follows that there is exactly one way to get him to do it. I do not think that is a consoling thought. I think it is a true one, and I have been carrying it around for two years, and this is what I have done with it.

GLOSSARY
Amu Nowruz [a-MOO now-ROOZ] — Persian, Uncle New Year. The figure who arrives at the spring equinox. In the story, Naneh
Sarma waits for him all year, falls asleep, and misses him.
Behesht-e Zahra [be-HESHT-e zah-RAA] — Tehran's principal cemetery, in the far south of the city.
Dallal [da-LAAL] — Arabic via Persian, broker, middleman. A fixer who takes a percentage on any transaction.
Delgoshā [del-go-SHAA] — Persian, heart-opening. Cheering, delightful; used of gardens and views. Also a family name, and the title of Obeid Zakani's fourteenth-century collection of anecdotes.
Enghelab [en-ghe-LAAB] — Arabic via Persian, revolution. A major avenue in central Tehran, and the university district.
Halva [hal-VAA] — a dense saffron sweet made of flour, oil, sugar and rosewater, prepared specifically for mourning and distributed at funerals.
Javadiyeh [ja-vaa-dee-YEH] — a neighbourhood in the south of
Tehran. Known among its own young men as Texas.

Javānmardi [ja-vaan-mar-DEE] — Persian, young-manliness. The old code of the street brotherhoods and the wrestling houses: generosity, courage, faithfulness to one's own, and turning a blind eye to another's faults.
Karaj [ka-RAJ] — a large city immediately west of Tehran.
Khanoom [khaa-NOOM] — Persian, lady, madam. A respectful form of address for a woman, used in place of a name.
Konkur [kon-KOOR] — from the French concours. The Iranian national university entrance examination.
Maddahi [mad-daa-HEE] — Arabic via Persian, eulogising.
Devotional chanting recalling the events of Karbala, performed at religious gatherings including funerals.

Majles-e tarhim [MAJ-les-e tar-HEEM] — Arabic via Persian, assembly of mercy. The principal memorial gathering, usually held in the side hall of a mosque, comprising Quran recitation, a clergyman's address, maddahi, and a reception of tea, dates and halva.
Naneh Sarma [naa-neh sar-MAA] — Persian, Grandma Frost. A figure of folklore who waits each year for Amu Nowruz and falls asleep before he arrives.
Narmak [nar-MAK] — a district in the east of Tehran.
Nowruz [now-ROOZ] — Persian, new day. The Iranian new year, at the spring equinox.
Piroozi [pee-roo-ZEE] — Persian, victory. A long avenue and district in eastern Tehran.
Resāleh [reh-saa-LEH] — Arabic via Persian, treatise. A short prose work on a single subject.
Resāleh-ye Delgoshā [reh-saa-LEH-ye del-go-SHAA] — The

Heart-Delighting Treatise. Obeid Zakani, mid-fourteenth century: short anecdotes satirising judges, preachers and the conspicuously pious. Extensively obscene, and bowdlerised in most editions printed since, the omissions marked with rows of dots.
Robāb [ro-BAAB] — a short-necked bowed or plucked string instrument of Persian and Central Asian music. Robabeh
[ro-baa-BEH] is a woman's name formed from it.
Sabur [sa-BOOR] — Arabic via Persian, patient, enduring. The conventional first adjective in eulogies for women.
Sāderāt mamnū' [saa-de-RAAT mam-NOO] — Persian, export forbidden. Standard prohibition signage.
Semnan [sem-NAAN] — a city and province east of Tehran.
Shahr-e Rey [shahr-e REY] — an ancient city, now the southernmost district of Tehran.
Sharif [sha-REEF] — Sharif University of Technology, Tehran.
Zakāni, Obeid [o-BAYD zaa-kaa-NEE] — c. 1300–1371. Persian poet and satirist from Qazvin. Author of the Resāleh-ye
Delgoshā, of Akhlāq al-Ashrāf, and of Mush-o-Gorbeh, in which a cat makes a public repentance and eats the mice who come to congratulate him.
